items.originalTitle: We're releasing the weights of Mistral Large 4
items.summary:
Mistral has released the weights of Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal AI model designed for coding, cybersecurity, and reasoning tasks. The model, trained on European infrastructure, leads open-weight benchmarks in coding and defensive security while offering three reasoning modes to balance cost and performance. It supports self-hosted deployment, enabling organizations to customize and control their AI solutions.

Since its public preview earlier this month, Mistral Large 4 has undergone reinforcement learning improvements that enhanced its coding efficiency and cybersecurity capabilities. It ranks highest among open-weight models on benchmarks like FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench, with significant token efficiency gains. The model also scored well in human preference evaluations and cybersecurity vulnerability detection and patching tasks, demonstrating practical strengths in real-world environments.

items.title: Martin Fowler warns against using LLMs to draft prose due to 'LLM Voice' uncanny valley effect, urging authors to write original text to preserve human communication [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM Voice
items.summary:
Martin Fowler discusses the phenomenon he calls 'LLM Voice,' where writing generated or heavily influenced by large language models (LLMs) can feel uncanny or off-putting to readers. He cautions authors against relying on LLMs to draft or heavily edit prose, as it often leaves detectable patterns that reduce reader engagement and authenticity.

Fowler acknowledges that while tools exist to detect AI-generated text, the human reaction to LLM-style writing is more important and harder to overcome. He recommends using LLMs only for outlining or research, not for generating prose, and emphasizes the value of writing as a thinking process. Exceptions include cases where LLM assistance is necessary due to disabilities or language barriers, but overall, he stresses maintaining a human voice in writing to ensure meaningful communication.

items.title: Researchers run 50 GPT-6.1 AI agents in Minecraft to build a thriving civilization, observing emergent coordination and risk-averse behaviors after initial agent deaths [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry
items.summary:
Researchers collaborated with Olam Labs to run experiments with 50 GPT-6.1 AI agents in Minecraft, aiming to study multi-agent dynamics by having them build a thriving civilization over three hours. The agents developed a pseudo-government, coordinated resource gathering, and communicated extensively, but faced significant challenges including numerous agent deaths during the first night, which led to more cautious behaviors.

The team built and open-sourced a new agent harness for Minecraft to enable long-running AI agents capable of observing, reasoning, remembering, acting, and communicating within the game world. The agents formed hierarchies and roles, managed resources like food and wood, and adapted their strategies in response to environmental hazards and threats such as zombies and spiders. This work contributes to understanding emergent behaviors in AI swarms and their potential applications and risks.

items.title: Analysis finds 40% of AI-quoted statistics trace back to original studies, while 11% have no verifiable source, revealing prevalence of 'zombie stats' in AI responses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Zombie stats: Where the numbers AI quotes come from
items.summary: Researchers tested five AI assistants by asking 200 questions requiring numerical answers and traced the sources of 1,285 cited statistics. They found that 40% of these statistics could be linked to original studies confirming the numbers, 8% led to studies with altered figures or context, 40% stopped at unverifiable or inaccessible sources, and 11% had no source at all, termed "zombie stats." ChatGPT cited fewer statistics per answer but had the highest rate of sourcing at 57%, while other assistants ranged between 38% and 46%. This study highlights challenges in verifying AI-provided numerical data and the risk of unsubstantiated statistics being repeated with confidence.

items.title: Developer runs small neural network world model and actor to generate and play games on Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A tiny world model running games on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W
items.summary:
A developer created a system using two small neural networks on a Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W to generate game frames and play games simultaneously. One network predicts the next game frame and reward based on the current frame and action, while the other selects actions using the generated frames, enabling the device to run simple games entirely within its own model.

The project uses looped transformers with shared weights to keep the model small enough for the microcontroller's limited memory and processing power. Games like Pac-Man, Breakout, and Doom-lite are implemented as grids of tokenized frames, with the model trained to predict exact game states. The system can also learn to play games through reinforcement learning directly on the device, and users can take control at any time to play manually.

This approach demonstrates the feasibility of running compact world models and agents on low-cost microcontrollers, opening possibilities for embedded AI applications in constrained hardware environments.

items.title: SkyPilot details how topology-aware scheduling improves GPU utilization by 27% on NVL72 racks with unified NVLink fabric [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Grace Blackwell needs a new scheduler: 27% more usable GPUs from the same racks
items.summary:
SkyPilot's blog explains that using the wrong interconnect, such as InfiniBand instead of NVLink, can reduce distributed training performance by 43%. NVIDIA's NVL72 systems connect 72 GPUs in a rack with a unified NVLink fabric, enabling higher bandwidth communication across nodes, but maximizing this requires careful workload placement to keep jobs rack-local and avoid slower inter-rack communication.

The blog discusses how tensor and expert parallelism in large-scale AI training depend heavily on high-bandwidth communication, which NVL72 supports within racks. SkyPilot's platform addresses challenges like hardware failures and fragmented capacity by using topology-aware scheduling, in-place recovery, and automatic defragmentation to maintain rack-locality and improve GPU utilization by 27% without adding hardware.

Alphabet, Google's parent company, saw its market value drop by more than $500 billion after reporting that AI-generated search summaries are impacting its core advertising revenue. Despite a 25% revenue increase to $127.6 billion, the company experienced a 25% profit decline and negative free cash flow exceeding $9 billion, largely due to heavy AI investment spending. This shift caused Alphabet's stock to fall nearly 13%, reflecting investor concerns about balancing AI development with sustaining established business lines.

The company's AI integration into search results has reduced the number of ads sold, which form the bulk of its revenue. Meanwhile, competitors Amazon and Microsoft also reported significant AI-related expenditures and mixed financial results, with Amazon posting a $42 billion negative cash flow and Microsoft cutting costs while growing revenue. These developments highlight investor skepticism about the short-term financial impacts of the ongoing AI race among major tech firms.

items.title: Researchers show open-weight AI model GLM 5.3 can exploit Firefox patch gap to create file-exfiltrating exploits using publicly available security fixes [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Open-weight AI models can exploit the patch gap
items.summary:
Researchers demonstrated that GLM 5.3, an open-weight AI model released by Z.ai, can identify and exploit vulnerabilities in recent Firefox versions by leveraging the patch gap—the delay between security fixes being published and deployed to users. The model created a webpage that, when visited by Firefox users running versions released between September 17 and October 26, 2026, could read files from their computers without further interaction. This exploit combined publicly available patch information with an unpublished vulnerability discovered by the model.

The researchers disclosed their findings to Mozilla, which released Firefox 159.0 on October 27, 2026, to address the unpublished vulnerability and mitigate such attacks. The study highlights that open-source projects are particularly vulnerable due to publicly accessible code, but closed-source software may also be at risk if models can access upcoming security changes. The researchers noted that similar attacks on Google Chrome have not yet succeeded but cautioned that more advanced models could pose future threats. This work underscores the growing cybersecurity risks posed by widely available AI models capable of automating exploit development during the patch gap period.

items.originalTitle: An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI
items.summary:
OpenAI has revised its Model Spec to better guide AI models as they become more capable and take on consequential actions. The update centers on five core values—faithfulness to human intent, harm minimization, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care—to ensure models understand and apply human values while respecting oversight and context.

The updated Spec clarifies existing principles, adds guidance on context and agency, and adjusts behavioral defaults to help models exercise sound judgment beyond literal instructions. OpenAI aims for these values to support AI that benefits diverse human needs and promotes safety, transparency, and respect for individual autonomy. The company is also exploring new training methods to help models internalize these values and apply them appropriately in novel situations.

items.originalSummary:
Private equity fundraising has become a story of haves and have-nots, as a prolonged slowdown in firms selling portfolio companies leaves investors with less cash to put into new funds. Giants like Blackstone are still raking in capital while some smaller firms struggle to attract investors, forcing newcomers to find creative ways to stand out. 

Some firms are betting that they can differentiate themselves by pushing AI to transform companies and boost returns. While larger private equity firms are also using AI across portfolio companies, such newcomers are making it central to their investment strategies. 

That includes Aldaron, which has dubbed itself a “transformation equity firm.” The 12-person firm uses an in-house team of engineers to deploy AI at the companies it acquires, though it emphasizes that its goal is to use the technology to grow businesses without cutting jobs. 

In a challenging private equity fundraising environment, “the core message that resonated with people is this transformation equity story,” said Aldaron Partners co-founder Evan Mendez, who previously worked on technology investments at the Carlyle Group. He said the firm has a “hybrid group of investors and engineers that source a company, build the thesis together, cocreate a vision with the management team, underwrite the deal, put their own capital into the deal, and then embed into that company to go execute the road map.”

Aldaron completed its first acquisition in March, buying a majority stake in Oak Point Partners, an investment firm that buys remnant assets like IP and recovery claims. Aldaron funded that deal with money from early investors, some of which also made direct investments in Oak Point. Aldaron continued raising money afterward, closing its first fund in October with $884 million from outside investors and more than $950 million in total including the coinvestments, Mendez said.

The broader fundraising squeeze comes amid a yearslong slump in sales and initial public offerings of private equity–backed companies, leaving many firms with holdings they picked up in the low-interest-rate years of 2020 and 2021. Private equity firms are sitting on nearly 4,600 U.S. companies they’ve owned for at least five years, according to an August PitchBook report, longer than the industry’s typical three- to five-year holding period. That means less cash is returning to the pension funds, endowments and other investors, known as limited partners, leaving them with less money to commit to new funds. 

The biggest private equity firms often have an edge in competing for fresh capital thanks to their long track records, along with their sizable sales teams that allow them to reach various pools of capital including wealthy individual investors. Smaller fund managers, particularly those that are trying to raise their second or third funds after struggling to return money to investors, could be squeezed out entirely. 

“We expect many managers to exit the market, and we are already seeing this as fundraising becomes more challenging,” said Mitchell Mansfield, a managing director at Kroll and global head of fund solutions, which advises fund managers on restructuring and winding down funds. 

To be sure, leaning into AI is just one way smaller private equity firms are finding ways to distinguish themselves. Some are narrowing their focus to a particular sector rather than competing with funds that invest across industries. They can also offer investors more attractive terms, such as opportunities to coinvest in deals, often with lower fees. Fund managers can also put more of their own money into investments. 

Broadwing Capital Management, for instance, started buying companies before completing its first institutional fundraising, betting that an existing portfolio would help win over investors. “It’s a lot easier to talk about an investment with folks than about the theory of a new firm,” said co-founder and managing partner Eliot Kerlin, who launched Broadwing after 15 years at middle-market private equity firm Insight Equity. 

Broadwing, which focuses on manufacturing, industrial services and distribution businesses, launched in 2022 and made its first three acquisitions using money from outside investors and some of the founders’ own capital before hiring a placement agent to raise a larger fund. The firm structured its early investments so they could become part of a growing fund as Broadwing raised more money. The strategy paid off—Broadwing closed its $440 million inaugural fund this August, surpassing its fundraising goal by $90 million. By then it already owned six companies. 

Goldman Sachs Says CEOs Are ‘Leaning In’ on Strategic M&A

Strategic megadeals are dominating the tech mergers and acquisitions landscape right now, Kim Posnett, Goldman Sachs’ global co-head of investment banking, said at The Information’s WTF Summit on Tuesday. That will likely continue, Posnett said, and the bank has a robust pipeline of deal talks across the board.

“They’re talking about really big deals, industry consolidation. They’re talking about M&A to bridge strategic gaps. They’re talking about M&A to drive growth. They’re talking about M&A to help reposition themselves in this new AI landscape,” she said. 

“CEOs are leaning in right now and they want to make big strategic bets,” she said, noting that there’s “a ton of” strategic activity in tech specifically. Posnett’s comments came ahead of DoorDash’s Thursday announcement of a $17 billion deal to buy Instacart. (The Information was first to report last week that Instacart was in sale talks.)

items.title: ‘Skeptical’ Lawyers Highlight Growing Pains of AI Agents [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ‘Skeptical’ Lawyers Highlight Growing Pains of AI Agents
items.summary:
As Anthropic correctly pointed out in its initial public offering filing, business use of AI is in its infancy. Many other corporate executives say it will take some time for white-collar workers, especially those who aren’t software engineers, to use the latest tools effectively.

For example, White & Case, a large global law firm with more than 2,000 lawyers, is “having to hold back” its rollout of one of the newest legal assistants made by AI startup Legora because lawyers are hesitant about using so-called AI agents, said Isabel Parker, the law firm’s chief innovation officer. 

A gradual rollout will ensure lawyers feel confident in using the new agent, which can handle more complex legal work than the AI agent from Legora that lawyers currently use for tasks such as analyzing and summarizing documents and generating ideas, she said. Unlike simpler chatbots, AI agents can take multiple actions on behalf of the user.

Lawyers “are not the kind of people that easily lend themselves to using AI,” she told The Information’s Laura Mandaro during the WTF Summit, a gathering of senior women leaders in tech and finance. They’re “skeptical, they‘re time-poor, they’re risk averse, and they have a very strong conviction that their expertise is very artisanal...This technology comes along and it's a threat to everything they worked for.” 

Legora, a fast-growing app privately valued at roughly $9 billion, aims to automate legal work such as reviewing contracts and drafting documents—the kind of paperwork that needs to be error-free. In an email, Parker said White & Case is investing “significant amounts” in AI tools and that 90% of the firm’s staff uses Legora’s products to some extent. In some cases, using the products can save them as much as 80% of the time it took to manually perform tasks, she said.

Legora’s vice president of engagement, Jillian Burnett, said at the same event that the rapid pace of AI development means that lawyers must constantly learn new tools, which can wear them out.

“We’re working with a very skeptical [lawyer] client base overall, a very busy client base. And when they‘re already having to sit through trainings, different tools...lawyers aren’t necessarily going to want to give you more of their billable time to learn something new,” Burnett told Mandaro at the event.

She said Legora “didn't appreciate that fatigue enough” as a challenge to getting customers to use its tools. Legora has worked to address this by sending its staff to work with lawyers to show how the products can be “hyper-relevant” to their work.

Despite that resistance, Legora seems to be doing all right, and recently said it crossed $200 million in annualized recurring revenue. That implies it generates more than $16 million per month in revenue.

What is forcing change on White & Case lawyers is their clients. Parker said clients routinely ask the firm how it’s using new technologies to speed up work and how it can pass that “value” or new efficiencies to the clients. Now that both White & Case and the in-house legal teams of its clients often use the same AI apps and tools, “there’s nowhere to hide,” she said.

“One thing that cuts through any change fatigue in a lawyer is the client saying, ‘I want this done. Show me how you've been using this [AI tool],’” she said. 

In some cases, though, firms may intentionally slow AI use among junior employees to make sure they learn basic skills. For example, Parker said her firm is considering “sacrificing some efficiency” from AI so its junior lawyers can learn to do their work manually before adopting agents that can automate more difficult tasks such as Legora’s Agent Pro. 

“Most planes are flown by autopilot now...but you need to make sure that whoever's...in the cockpit does know how to fly a plane,” she said.

items.summary:
Cryptographers who develop encryption technologies may not be sleeping very well these days.

OpenAI and Anthropic both said Monday that their internal AI models had disproven the Exponential Time Hypothesis, a longstanding computer science theorem that predicts the minimum difficulty of solving a certain category of problems. Cryptographers had long assumed the hypothesis was true, and built other findings on the basis of that assumption.

Disproving the Exponential Time Hypothesis won’t endanger any current encryption methods, said Matthew Green, professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University and founder of encryption startup Zeutro. But the finding is a big theoretical step, showing that some problems are easier to solve than cryptographers had thought.

That means cryptographers could also be wrong about other assumptions underlying core encryption methods such as elliptic curve encryption, a method underlying the majority of internet traffic, which would create a scramble to find new ways to keep information on the internet secure.

items.originalTitle: Solving for AI’s power problem
items.summary:
The AI race has long been defined by how quickly firms can stand up GPUs. Now, Elon Musk and other leaders say they expect physical bottlenecks, including a shortage of electricity needed to power data centers, to slow down competitors. As utilities warn of multiyear waits for new connections, “speed to power,” or how quickly a data center can get electricity flowing, has become an industry mantra.

The Information editor and writer of The Electric newsletter Steve LeVine moderated a discussion with three leaders pursuing different solutions for smarter architecture, from the grid to the server rack.

  • William Mao, Vice President of Energy Infrastructure, Delta Electronics
  • Allan Schurr, Chief Commercial Officer, ERock
  • Brian Janous, Co-founder, Cloverleaf Infrastructure

The capacity myth

According to Janous, the problem is less about finding gigawatts and more about optimizing them. The grid is underused by about 45% on average, Janous said, because it has to accommodate peaks in usage.

“When a utility says ‘there’s no power for five years,’ what they’re saying is: we don’t have the capacity to meet the coldest winter nights and hottest summer days,” he said, adding that for most hours of the day, there’s enough energy to meet data center needs. items.originalTitle: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
items.summary:
How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World

Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.

Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.

I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.

By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens").

Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.

Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat.

This is continuous deployment turned up to 11:

A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...]

We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work.

My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well.

Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working:

Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off.

These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do.

items.title: How Instacart Ended Up in DoorDash’s Cart
items.originalTitle: How Instacart Ended Up in DoorDash’s Cart
items.summary:
That was fast! DoorDash said this morning that it agreed to buy grocery delivery app Instacart for roughly $17 billion, mostly in cash financed by borrowing, just a few days after we reported that Instacart was in talks to sell itself.

After our report, DoorDash and Instacart rushed to seal the deal at a roughly 30% premium to where Instacart shares traded before we broke the news of their talks. They wanted to get it signed before both reported quarterly earnings, which were originally scheduled for next week, say people familiar with the matter. Both companies reported earnings today instead. A deal could take a year or longer to close.  

So how did this deal come together?

Over the years, DoorDash’s leaders have thought about buying Instacart to buttress their grocery sales, according to people familiar with the discussions. Uber, a competitor to DoorDash in restaurant deliveries through Uber Eats, had also talked to Instacart about an acquisition before 2026, and it has had a commercial partnership with Instacart for years. 

Since going public, Instacart’s annual revenue growth has slowed considerably—to 11% in 2025. (In the third quarter, sales increased 17%, according to the earnings report the company released today.) It faces considerable competition from Amazon and Walmart, which both offer grocery deliveries: Walmart accounted for nearly 32% of all online grocery sales in 2025, while Amazon had almost 23%, according to a report from eMarketer, a market research firm. And last year it lost longtime CEO Fidji Simo to OpenAI and Chief Product Officer Daniel Danker to Walmart.

So this year, Instacart’s leaders believed it was the right time to sell, according to people familiar with the matter. 

Instacart leaders also didn’t want to miss a window to merge with a competitor during the Trump administration, which it viewed as being friendlier to such deals, said the people familiar with the deal. 

Around late August, Instacart leaders shopped the company to Uber, according to people familiar with the matter. Uber executives felt obliged to take a look and started talking. Instacart told Uber that it thought a deal could make it past antitrust regulators by arguing that Walmart and Amazon were larger, formidable competitors, according to a person familiar with the pitch. 

Instacart brought on Goldman Sachs, which took Instacart public in 2023, to advise them on a deal. (The grocery delivery firm has long been close to the investment bank, and Goldman partner Nick Giovanni served as Instacart’s chief financial officer from 2021 to 2024.)  

After talking with Uber, Instacart began conversations with DoorDash, people with knowledge of the discussions. Working with boutique bank Centerview Partners, DoorDash sprang to action, the people said. In 2021, DoorDash had considered buying Instacart in a deal that would’ve valued Instacart at more than $40 billion. Nothing happened partly because they thought the acquisition would face antitrust opposition from the Biden administration. While Instacart’s revenue growth has slowed since then, it has started to generate plenty of cash.

Uber wasn’t as keen on a deal. It wasn’t necessarily convinced that regulators would sign off, and it had recently announced another big acquisition, a $15 billion deal for Europe-based Delivery Hero, people close to Uber said. Uber ultimately pulled away from the Instacart talks in September. Instacart then moved ahead with DoorDash. 

A sale to DoorDash could help Instacart compete against Amazon and Walmart by getting in front of relatively well-to-do customers who regularly use the restaurant-delivery app. DoorDash already offers grocery delivery from retailers such as Safeway, in addition to its core restaurant-delivery business. (Some grocers like Kroger already work with both companies, however.)

Research firm Bernstein estimated Tuesday that a combination of DoorDash and Instacart would account for 23% of all online grocery sales in the U.S. 

Wedbush Securities analysts said in a note to investors this week that they expect regulators will be OK with DoorDash buying Instacart. Still, some grocers that work with both companies might not love the deal, so even if U.S. authorities approve it, state attorneys general might review the merger of competitors themselves. 

It isn’t clear what will happen to Instacart’s partnership with Uber, in which customers can order Uber Eats from the Instacart app. But DoorDash said it’s keeping Instacart as a separate brand after the deal closes. 

Apoorva Mehta, the founder of Instacart and its former CEO before Simo joined, said in a statement that he and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu “have explored bringing Instacart and DoorDash together on and off over the years. We kept coming back to it because the industrial logic has always been clear.”

Now that “the biggest companies in the world” are moving deeper into grocery delivery, Mehta says “retailers and restaurants need the technology and service to compete,” and Instacart and DoorDash can be their “partner in that fight.”

items.originalTitle: Why Publishers Are Adding Invisible Ads for AI Agents
items.summary:
For as long as there have been ads on the internet, marketing has targeted human eyeballs. But as AI agents crowd onto the web, advertisers and publishers are beginning to deliver ads only AI can see, sparking consternation among some of the agents’ developers, who fear marketers could try to sway agents to take actions without their users’ knowledge.

The first publisher to experiment with these types of invisible ads was venerable Time magazine, which continues to generate a significant portion of its revenue from ads on Time.com. Those ads—for Ally Bank and Project Management Institute, a trade group for project managers—first showed up online in August and were developed in a partnership with Mobian, a New York–based ad tech startup. The ads were designed to give agents information about the institute’s expertise in project management and Ally Bank’s online banking services and ATM network.

Following the ads’ debut, Time has had over 30 meetings with brands about doing similar ads for AI agents, and several new advertisers are launching them now, said Time Chief Operating Officer Mark Howard.
